utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi to continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Before we talk in detail about the events following the explosion on the 28th of August, 1995, just two very, very small issues. You told us yesterday about that rescue operation, as I perhaps should call it, of members of the Russian battalion, and you said that you successfully arranged a cease-fire among the participants. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. For a short interval a time it was necessary to pull out the soldiers from the Russian observation post from under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that cease-fire was successful and the operation could be concluded?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember whom you contacted from the warring factions, from the ABiH and from the SRK?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very highest level I was assisted by General Gobillard, who with his staff contacted with the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina so that I myself did not contact with anyone. I know that these agreements came down to the commander of the 1st Corps and down to the lowest level of the relevant company, and I don't know which commanders of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were involved, but I know that at my request the liaison officer contacted them. The commander of the corps passed on the orders all the way down to the company and the relevant units to stop fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the commander of the corps would be Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. The second issue is about your knowledge about all these weapon systems as you had explained yesterday. I believe also in response to a question by Judge Harhoff. Now, you know as much about mortars and artillery as you know about tanks and all the other arsenal of the weaponry you were trained in and you had under your disposition while commanding all these units.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you're not really a sort of hundred per cent specialist only in mortars. You're a specialist about the whole range of -- of weaponry. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I am a general army commander who has to know everything and who has to have all the skills to command subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. Now, let's go into the beef of your testimony, and this is the 28th of August. Obviously we knew about your activities because it was widely reported. You know, people talk about your name, and it's mentioned in a couple of communications. Also in this courtroom your name was mention by various participants. But at least for me it's the first time I kind of got the sequence of what you were doing at any time, and I'd like to -- to go back to a few of these activities you conducted. You told us, I believe, that when the explosion happened you were at the -- your headquarters, which is the PTT building in Sarajevo. Is that correct? Morning of the 28th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What were you doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot reconstruct these events up to the minute, but at that time I was usually in a briefing. That was my regular schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how long between you hearing of the event by whatever means of communication and going to the crater, how much time was there in between?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: An hour and a half, I think, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why did you decide, if you recall today, to go to see the crater?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was too tragic an event to leave it without supervision, regardless of all my subordinates were doing. I had to see it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you told us yesterday that there were other specialised groups in UNPROFOR who were better equipped to go there, and we also had the UN observers who were on the scene. Are you saying that you just felt as the chief of staff you needed to go there and perhaps show presence at the scene?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. May I just ask that if Mr. Waespi is invoking a passage from the witness's testimony or statement, if he could indicate which one, such as, for instance, if he says the witness had said that there were better-equipped teams, which I personally don't remember, he might want to refer us to the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this was yesterday. I mean, if the witness don't recall saying it, then we can ask for the citation, but if the witness himself doesn't challenge it, I don't myself see the need for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe he didn't use the word "better."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think you said that there were specialised teams who would normally attend to scenes like that. I don't want to put words into your mouth. Perhaps, Colonel, you can explain what you meant by these other units who were available.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, in every unit of the UNPROFOR, including battalions, including military observers, everyone had their own area of responsibility, and if anything happened in that area they were the first who had to go there and see what happened. So my personal decision to scout for myself did not have anything to do with lack of trust in them. I decided to go because it was a tragic event with a gigantic number of casualties and that's why I thought I would go and see for myself before taking any steps. At that moment, I didn't know that I would personally lead an inquiry team. I just wanted to go and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said you arrived at around one and a half hours after the incident, which would be, I think, at around half past 12.00. For how long did you stay at the location?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to stay on this a moment longer. In your previous question you asked me how much time after you were alerted, not how much time after the event, and I answered an hour and a half. I was alerted 30 minutes later, then plus another hour and a half. That makes two hours. So it was not at 12.00. It was a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks for the clarification. And it's not a memory test. I just want to get some feeling of when you arrived and who you perhaps might have met there, because yesterday you told us that you gave instructions to UNPROFOR people working at the site. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, who were these UNPROFOR people working at the site to whom you gave instructions? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, I can't recall either the name or the numbers of battalions who worked there, but there were at least two groups, one from the FrenchBat, one from the military observers. They cordoned off -- or, rather, taped off the site, the scene, and proceeded to look very carefully for evidence, especially for shrapnel fragments stuck in buildings and elsewhere. I gave everyone a precise assignment indicating the time allowed and the deadline for reports, but I cannot remember the details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The other group of UNMOs, was that a group headed by Lieutenant Colonel Konings, the Dutch UNMO patrol leader?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, possibly. I cannot say for sure but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember, just in a general sense, what kind of assignment, if any, you gave to Lieutenant Colonel Konings?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I was not authorised to give him any assignments because military observers are a separate section of the UNPROFOR, of the UN force, that was not directly subordinated either to the commander of the sector or the chief of staff. They are a separate branch and that's why they are called independent military observers. But in terms of cooperation, I spoke to the UNMO officer trying to define what was necessary to do first and within what time. I couldn't give him orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification, but can you tell me more in substance of what did you tell him he has to do?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, things unfolded approximately like this: We introduced ourselves to each other. We defined the tasks handled by various groups, by the two groups, in fact, and we exchanged a few words about what our assignments were, within what time they were to be performed, and approximately when the reports would follow. Again, I have to emphasise I couldn't issue any orders because they were not my underlings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes I understand that very, very well but you're talking about coordination, and I just want to make sure I know what kind of coordination you had focusing now on Lieutenant Colonel Konings. So what coordination from your side or what did you tell him you were doing, if anything?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe the witness answered already twice. The question is asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think the witness said that, We exchanged a few words about what our assignments were, within what time they were to be performed and approximately when the reports would follow. And what I'd like to know is what -- an exchange means Mr. Konings set his side and Colonel Demurenko his side. I just want to know what Colonel Demurenko relate to lieutenant Colonel Konings about his assignment, what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness answer. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me draw your attention to one thing. I am not confirming that I talked to Colonel Konings. I said I spoke to an officer from the UNMO. I am not confirming the identity of that person. So please phrase your questions relating to a military observer and not Colonel Konings because I don't know the person for sure. This was general talk, I'm saying once again, about what the observers were doing as their part of the work and which other part of the work had to be done by other people, including me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in relation to the other unit that was there, the French unit, you had similar kind of exchanges between -- as regards to assignments and time frames?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. In the same context.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there at the crater site?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifteen, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was somebody with you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was accompanied by Captain Tyulenev, who was my driver and my bodyguard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then you returned back to -- to the headquarters, to the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when did you find out about this press conference, the British -- I think you said British UNPROFOR spokesperson gave?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What stuck in my memory is the impression I got when I came back to my headquarters in the PTT building approximately an hour after my visit to the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me. Colonel, the last question from counsel begs the question of whether you, when you visited the site the first time, whether you were given any indication as to the direction of fire and the angle of descent. So in other words when you came back to your headquarters, were you by then offered any information as to where the shot might have come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the moment when I was on the scene there were no documents available. The place of explosion itself. It did not indicate anything, it did not provide any clues as to who could have been the perpetrator of that tragedy. We had nothing at that time. Only towards the evening when I got information on one hand from the press conference, and on the other hand I got the two reports that I held in my hands during the video footage we've seen. It became clear that these two reports were mutually contradictory. The spokesman who had no information about preliminary results of inquiry made his statement, and on the other hand I still did not have enough information to refute the preliminary findings. I had those reports which indicated the angle of descent and some other clues. MR. WAESPI: Thank you, Mr. President -- just following up -- thank you, Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just following up on Judge Harhoff's question, why there were no documents that were created at that time, or perhaps you were not aware of any, from the cater itself, looking at the crater itself, analysing the crater as the French unit and perhaps the Dutch, you can indeed discover the angle descent and the bearing, the general bearing from which the shell, if it indeed was a flying shell, came from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without special tools and instruments there is not a chance you can determine the exact angle. This is the work of ballistics experts and specialists in gunnery and various forms of ammunition. All you can see is the trace on the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but you have seen, and you showed to the press, and yesterday you, I think, referred to the same document that you can make calculations that relate to the impact of the projectile to the vicinity of the buildings. You make calculations, and you come to conclusion about the angle of descent of a specific projectile.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's only when you have in front of you reports from specialists who used specialised tools in their work, who calculated possible angles of descent. Only with that, using firing tables, taking into account that angle and the bearings can you chart the line which allows you to check possible firing points. That is the only way. You cannot go any other way. It has to start with the work of ballistics experts who worked with appropriate instruments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The work you did and others did later about the possible charges, about the possible origins of fire, that's a different story, but the bearing, the approximate direction where the fire came from, and the angle of descent, that can be done with margin of error, of course, but the general elements can be done fairly, fairly quickly looking at the crater, measuring the distances between the impact and the height of the buildings, give you a very, very good indication, not perfect, about the angle of descent and the general direction where the shell came from. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can make some virtual models in your head, but in such a situation that took so many human lives, that is simply not fair, not appropriate. If I reconstructed in my head a virtual angle of descent, that would mean nothing. It would give nothing, no indication of involvement on either the Serbian or Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I agree that at the end it has to be a proper investigation, but the only point I'm making, that given the fairly clear crater on the ground and other elements, perhaps other information the UNMOs had about hearing sounds, it was possible to make a preliminary determination about the bearing and the direction of fire. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't. No information about who heard what in terms of flying shells was available then. We saw that only later in reports. Believe me, when you see practically a vertical hole in the asphalt at an angle of 65 to 70 degrees, you cannot tell anything. I'm a professional man, and on that basis I can say nothing. My job was to organise teams and organise that work within a certain deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We did have experts who testified here that from the pattern you could see on the ground created by the projectile in whatever form it was fired, it -- you could see clearly the approximate direction around that hit the road by the shape of the pattern, but we don't need to go further into that, although we might come back later. Let's talk about this press conference. Did you attend the press conference of the UNPROFOR gentleman?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. To me it came as a surprise, and it was a very reckless move on his part if you ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So how did you find out about the press conference?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military organisation everybody is in constant contact with one another, from the superior commander of the ABiH and from the other side. There is a constant flow of information towards my superiors. Reports come on my desk all the time, and I saw one of them quoting the words of the spokesman about an alleged Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that person who relayed that information to you, was that somebody from the ABiH side or from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no contacts with the Serbian side, and I wasn't supposed to have any, unless you are referring to the case with the Russian battalion. Of course it was as a subordinate officer. I don't remember his name exactly, but it's possible that he was our liaison officer with the media. He was duty-bound to inform me about all of the events that concerned the media and press releases, as well as contacts with the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So as I understand, he was part of your organisation. He was connected to you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. UNPROFOR staff, Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And he relayed to you what he heard at the press conference?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely he did not attend the press conference but just received a press release, which was a standard procedure. He received a hard copy of a press release, and he came and reported to me. I don't think that he attended the press conference because it was organised hastily, and it wasn't as comprehensive as it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall after so many years the approximate time the press conference was held or you received the information about the press conference?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was within an hour of my arrival at the headquarters. So if I arrived back at the headquarters at around 2.00, then at around 3.00 I received this information, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. And was it then that you decided now it's time for you to get more involved and -- and start your own investigation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was. I decided this in the evening. At that point in time I was enraged by the fact that somebody gave them right to indicate who the enemy was. They had no such right. As for the decision to head the investigation group, that decision emerged when two facts met in my head, namely that one person was lying and that I had in my hands reports that everybody would believe. One was the BH document, and the other document was the document of the Dutch officer about the angle of descent. When I realised that there were these two facts, I decided to head this investigation group. Perhaps if it weren't for these two facts, if both of them did not exist, I would not have taken this decision. I would have just thought, oh, right, somebody lied. A lot of people lie during wartime. And then I would have said, "All right, boys. Let us continue the work. We'll try to find the culprit." However, the existence of these two facts, when I realised this, it became obvious to me that I had to do something in order not to allow the truth to escape or at least not to allow the lie to triumph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm interested in these two reports which you have mentioned yesterday as well. You repeated that one report is by a Dutch officer, and I believe you yesterday said that the second report was by a Croat or a Bosnian source. So first the report of the Dutch officer. Again, you know, if you don't recall the names, that's fine, but just tell it us as much as you know about the report. Who authored it? How long was it? Can you tell us anything about that so we can perhaps identify together what report you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my mind you can see that in my hands in the video footage, you can see in that footage that I was holding something in my hands. I think there was the logo of the BH army on that document, a shell was drawn and also the angle of descent, and you should be able to trace this document in the archives of UNPROFOR. The other report was either Dutch or French, more likely it was the French report. I think that I held the French report in my hands, and in one of these two reports there was discussion of angle of descent, bearings. So those were the two documents that I held in my hands in that video footage, and you should be able to locate these documents in the UNPROFOR archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand now. So what you are saying is that the two reports you showed to the public during your press appearance, I think that was on 1st September were the same two reports that you have seen in the afternoon or evening on the 28th of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. The interview was given on the 2nd of September, not on the 1st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, during the night I went over the materials that the Prosecution wanted to introduce through this witness. However, this drawing, this document bearing logo of the BH army exists. I think that it was even admitted into evidence, but I wasn't able to trace it overnight. This photograph of a shell impacting the surface exists. It was introduced into evidence in this case, Your Honours. I was unable to find it last night, although I did my best. It was admitted into evidence through a witness, this document that this witness is referring to. I think that if we tried, both I and my learned friend, we should be able to trace the document. I saw it at least 10 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure I also think know what you are talking about. The only thing I want to make sure is that, because I'm now talking about two reports, the witness had looked at on the 28th of August after or before the press conference these two documents, one Dutch or French, the other one Bosnian or Croat. And the way I understand the witness, he's saying these are the same reports that he waved into the camera on the 2nd of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is that a fair characterisation of what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were precisely the documents, and I wanted just to make sure that it's clear that it was on the 2nd of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. I don't think you mentioned it yesterday, but we'll come to the sequence of events in a moment. Now, having seen the crater and having looked at the reports and having heard or read about the press conference, was that now the moment that you decided to form your group of -- of specialists to -- to look into the matter?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you told the Trial Chamber yesterday that you then went to see General Bachelet, who was your immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when did you do that? Can you tell us, because that's also something I couldn't find in any document. I'm not denying it took place, but can you tell us more about that when did you meet him where did you meet him? How long did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was either on the 28th or the 29th. I don't remember the exact date, but it wasn't earlier than the evening on the 28th, although it's also possible that it was on the following evening, the 29th. As for the briefing, yes, it lasted 10 to 15 minutes, not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was somebody else present?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Because as we know now, there was a military assistant who prevented you from seeing the general another time. This military assistant wasn't present this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we need to be more specific. Was that the first meeting or the second meeting? He's now speaking of the first meeting, and the second meeting took place later. I do not want to interfere, but could my learned friend Mr. Waespi first establish when the first meeting was held and then the time of the second meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I thought it was clear we are talking about the first time. The witness is sure whether it's on the evening of the 28th or the 29th August. The meeting lasted about 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I think you said, Colonel, that the military assistant was not present. It was just between you, the chief of staff, and General Bachelet.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where did that take place, in the office of General Bachelet at the PTT?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That did not take place at the headquarters. I don't remember where it was that I talked briefly to General Bachelet, but it was something that was improvised. I remember that clearly, because the issue arose spontaneously, and I sought an opportunity to discuss this with the general, to tell him that I wanted personally to take part in the investigation. In addition to this, it's possible that some details slipped my memory -- from my memory, and it's possible that this was a telephone discussion, not a meeting, an actual meeting, but I definitely made the suggestion to him and he gave me his response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi and Mr. Tapuskovic, the two reports that were mentioned, the Chamber would wish to see them. Mr. Tapuskovic says that in his recollection they were mentioned earlier in the case. Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning to you and Your Honours. The report, the Bosnian MUP, the police report, which is one of reports I believe the witness is speaking about was tendered through Witness 137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The exhibit number -- it was tendered in various parts. The diagram showing the wall and the angle of descent was P253 under seal. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- 53 under seal. The -- the picture of the shell showing the centre of explosion and how the angle of descent is calculated is P254 under seal, and the official MUP CSB report is 255 under seal which provides of list of wounded and deceased. And the other report, if it is indeed the Dutch -- Mr. Konings' report or the French report, the sector -- French sector cell report is P -- it's incorporated -- incorporated in P357.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the court deputy will get those reports for us. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honours, there is a drawing bearing the logo of the Muslim-Croat federation. There is a drawing showing this shell. It's a very clear, striking drawing. It was admitted into evidence. I remember seeing it. It's a drawing of the shell and the angle of impact. This is the drawing that this witness held in his hands. I know it exists. I was unable to find it because there was no time, but I'm sure that the Prosecution can find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's what I'm referring to. In fact, I have it up on my screen right now. It's P254 under seal and it shows the shell and it shows how the angle of descent is calculated and it has the minister of the interior of the Sarajevo -- the federation Ministry of Interior logo on the diagram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, yesterday I mentioned the Chamber's interest all these reports which the witness said he saw and which pointed to differing conclusions. I think he said perhaps six or eight reports, and you must be interested, I would imagine, in -- in those reports, because if you -- if you have six or eight reports from fairly credible sources, all with different conclusions, then that must throw some doubt on the Prosecution's case on this point, and so I would have thought you would have been interested in ascertaining from the witness precisely as -- giving information as precisely as he can, to identify these reports so that an effort could be made to find them, because it is occurring to me, at any rate, that the science and the technology in this area is not very -- not very precise, and the question I would have to ask myself as a Judge is how can I be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt about anything that is produced in this area. If so many reports have differing conclusions, what is the Chamber to believe? So for the beginning we will have the two reports which have been evidenced, and we will look at them. But the Chamber does have an interest in identifying with as much precision as is possible the other reports to which the witness referred, and to ascertain if they're available and to get them. Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might just add and hopefully it might resolve some issues. There are -- there are a series of reports that have been tendered in this case, in the Prosecution case. The three reports, the first one was the patrol report by Mr. Konings, followed on by the French report, the French sector cell report and indeed the Bosnian Muslim MUP report, and I know this is not the place to make closing arguments, but in our submission those three reports concluded that the bearing was roughly 160 to 180 degrees and the angle of descent was 67 minimum angle of descent through to 70 degrees. So in our submission there is no contradiction between those three reports. Now, there was a further G2 UNPROFOR report that was the result of a further investigation and as Mr. President and Your Honours have heard evidence, they came to a bearing of 220 to 240 degrees. And the Prosecution has produced witnesses, Bosnian MUP witnesses, expert witness Richard Higgs, and Mr. Konings who have all in our submission refuted the 220-240 bearing, because in our submission the crater analysis, the crater was very clear and you could only come to one conclusion, and I submit that you have heard that in our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is what I think I will want to do, and I will give instructions for this could be carried out: Each and every report that has been tendered by the Prosecution, I would like it to be placed before this witness and have his comments on it, and then he can tell us whether, having seen those reports, he saw other reports, and we'll make an effort to get them. So that exercise will be carried out at some time, and I'll ask the court deputy to liaise with the Prosecutor to identify all reports that have been tendered, and the Chamber will carry out that questioning of the witness. So let us continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We do have a list with all these several reports which can be given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. -- Let us -- let him finish. Do you want -- are you finished, or do you want to speak for him? Yes. Let Mr. -- All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to comment on what Mr. Sachdeva said. There was a third drawing. In addition to the first two drawings, there was also a third one, a third sketch. What Powers, Baxter and some others said was already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have given an instruction, and that instruction is to be carried out by the court deputy, the Chamber's legal assistant, with the help of the parties, and this is to be done by the -- by the break, which is at 9.30, and that instruction is to have ready a list of all the reports that were tendered in the Prosecution's case on this incident, and I'd like the witness to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Like Mr. Tapuskovic, Mr. Sachdeva also didn't sleep this night, he collected a list of these reports which can be e-mailed, I guess, to the Defence, to Mr. Monkhouse, and to the legal officer and it can be printed out. It lists the dates, the exhibit numbers, and even a couple of points about the conclusions, so I think we should be ready by the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Going back to the issue of you talking to General Bachelet perhaps over the phone, and you said that that might have been a spontaneous act. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But at the same time, you already have grouped your group of specialists who would help you to investigate.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group of specialists, actually my staff. I can call in anybody of them any minute. I did not assemble anyone until I actually spoke to General Bachelet. I simply thought about it in my head, about the steps that could be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe yesterday you said you offered to General Bachelet to do that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many people from your staff did assist you and please list the names. We can also go into private session if you want for that exercise so the names don't become public. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there is anything confidential here. I know for a fact that it was Captain Tyulenev and Major Kozhurov from the Russian unit of the Sarajevo sector staff. As for other officers, I called them in as necessary. For example, chief of engineering corps of the Russian battalion was called in by me so that he could assist in establishing whether there were any minefields in those location that we wanted to photograph, which we wanted to visit in our investigation. I also called in other officers as necessary, but I do not remember their last names. There were 5.000 people under my command, and it's impossible to remember all of their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the core group of people that worked with you, your bodyguard/driver, you mentioned him before, the other major and the chief of engineering, these were all nationals, citizens of Russia like you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: By the way, who was the chief of the Russian battalion at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forgot his last name. In the first part of the winter Lieutenant Colonel Boltikov was the commander and then starting in the spring and onwards, I forgot. He was a colonel of -- of airborne forces, and I forgot his last name, but it will come back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And it's not really --

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dvornikov, Dvornikov, Colonel Dvornikov.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when was it the first time you were sitting together, if at all, with this group of people or perhaps even with one to discuss these three actions you relayed to us yesterday, and we'll come to that in a moment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the investigation took approximately three days, we either assembled or dispersed in various directions. I first gave them the task to establish all the calculations on the first day, on the 28th, and then following that some people worked with the firing tables. Some people dealt with photographs and projecting possible flight trajectory of the shell. Then some people dealt with the location of minefields. Everybody did their own job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And at the end you had what told us yesterday, a report with conclusions, kind of collecting all this information others did in the course of their duties?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where's the report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report. In my personal archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could it be made available to the Court?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, although there is one problem. At least I thought of it as a problem until now. Before leaving for the Hague, thinking about how I would corroborate my testimony and arguments and knowing that I had in my personal archive some UNPROFOR documents that I took as a memento, I realised that there is a -- possibly a service related delicate problem. On some of those things that I took from the UNPROFOR, you have the stamp "Confidential." Other documents are not confidential. They are written in my own hand. I contacted somebody who specialises in international law, Baktier Muhamyedov [phoen] who used to be an advisor in the former Yugoslavia, to ask him whether the UN would enable me to produce those documents, and he said no, I had to ask for special permission from the UN staff to reveal them. So this is my personal dilemma. I have some useful documents in my archive, but I don't have them here. If it is not contrary to international law, I could make them available to the Court by courier, by regular mail, bring them myself. That is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We have seen many UN reports. This is confidential, this is 15 years ago, and there is a UN procedure which can be fairly quickly to declassify these documents, and I personally, having looked at so many UN reports here, see no issue about confidentiality, but of course that's up to -- I think it's the UN headquarters to look into these issues, and I'm really convinced that we could accommodate you in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see the issue either, and I'm very surprised that the report that you yourself prepared, you didn't bring here. I mean, this is the outcome of your investigations. So why didn't you bring it? I mean, even if you were to leave those reports which you felt you could not bring because in your view they were confidential, I mean, the basic report itself, which is the product of your work, why didn't you bring that? Because I mean that would certainly lend credibility to the story you have been telling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And if I my follow up on the President's questions. Why was your report never filed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the point is when I was called to the Tribunal I didn't know what I would be questioned about. It was a very broadly phrased invitation, something like this: "Colonel, could you possibly appear here as a witness to testify about events in the former Yugoslavia at the time when you were there?" And I said yes. But what exactly the subject of questioning would be, what I would need to produce to corroborate my testimony, nothing was specified. I simply brought here what I could bring through the door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's apparent to me that you'll have to return with the report and any other documents that you have. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Colonel, could you answer my question? It would seem to me that given the efforts you made at the time to ensure that a second opinion was offered even to the public about where the missile might have been launched from, if at all, given those efforts you would have an interest in securing at least that your report was kept on file. That is to say that you wouldn't just keep your own report for yourself but that you would have ensured that it was kept also in the UNPROFOR files. So why didn't you ensure that your report was properly filed with the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am absolutely in agreement with you. Moreover, I had been waiting a long time for somebody from the UNPROFOR, from the Sarajevo sector, from the UN BH command, for the UN in general to ask me while I was still there in Sarajevo, "Colonel, could you produce documents to confirm, to corroborate the information that you gave to Associated Press," but nobody uttered a word about it. Nobody ever asked me a thing. I heard from them only two things: "We will throw you out, or we will kill you." Exactly. Exactly. That was the only argument. And nobody asked a thing. It was undesirable information for everyone. Of course I would have been very pleased to share it. I would have been very pleased to file it, place it into archives, but I was rejected as a source of information leading in an unwanted direction. The truth, nobody wanted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I owe you an explanation. I believe I owe it because it would appear completely illogical I hadn't asked the witness to bring these documents and evidence. I had a contact with this witness a year ago, maybe 18 months ago, just enough to locate him and to elicit his consent to appear as a witness. Since that time I did not have any further discussions with him, and when it was decided in those 15 days to compile a 65 ter list of witnesses, it was approved for me to go to Moscow for a two- or three-day visit, but I couldn't do all the work to complete the 65 ter list, including all the exhibits, so I asked the Registry to bring this witness a day or two earlier than is the custom, and I had all my proofing with the witness in the past three or four days, and that's when I learned about the documents. I learned about those he showed during the interview, and now I hear for the first time that he has some more documents which are confidential, and I am really at a loss what to tell you. If I had seen this witness before the trial, I would have insisted that he bring these documents. That is the difficulty the Defence faced, and it is understandable that the Court insists on evidence that could give more credibility to the evidence presented by this witness. But if I had extended my stay in Moscow, I would have fallen short on some other duties that I had to complete in those 15 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, I believe -- I have to say that I don't fully agree with you. Since the beginning, you have questioned the Prosecution's position on this incident of the 28th of August, and it was your duty to get in touch with your witness and to ask him to bring all the documents with him, because if you do not have any documents on that particular incident, if you do not have any arguments or documents to counter the arguments presented by the Prosecution relating to incidents referred to in the indictment, then I believe your arguments are not very strong. I don't think you didn't have the time. I believe you did have the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Mindua, I must respond. I have a certain number of UN documents in my hands that demonstrate eloquently the things that this witness is testifying about, and I have shown them to the witness. These documents are self-explanatory. The problem here is that the witness is also in possession of some more UNPROFOR documents that I didn't know about before. I'm hearing it for the first time now. I didn't know that he had in his possession some UNPROFOR documents that are -- that are confidential. If those documents were not approved for disclosure by the UN, I wouldn't have asked him to reveal them to me even if I had known about them. So that I personally, as Defence counsel, don't think I need anything more. I'm speaking on my own behalf, of course, as counsel. And after the testimony of this witness and on the basis of evidence that were already admitted even before him, I as Defence counsel for Dragomir Milosevic need no further documents. If this witness can produce some more documents and the Court wants them, there is a certain procedure to declassify them. If I had known about them, and I didn't, I couldn't have asked the witness to produce them. He brought some other documents, photographs, two documents that have already been exhibited, et cetera, whereas the others that he says are confidential, I couldn't ask him to produce them here, but I know there is a procedure. The documents that I showed the witness are self-explanatory, and I don't think any further comment is needed. I'll leave it for closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a couple of clarification points about this report. I take it it's in Russian. The main -- your report is in Russian?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, a report is a compilation of documents. It's the -- there is no final detailed report because the entire conclusion boils down to one sentence. The statement made by the spokesman is false. This couldn't have been a shell from the Serb side. That's one sentence. All the rest was in my hands at that time. Firing tables, the maps, reports from other officers in Bosnia speaking of the angle descent, but there is no one finished final report. It is a compilation, including photographs of various locations showing that it was impossible to fire from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I understand there are various parts. There are these UNPROFOR reports which were in your possession and which you took into account. There are the Bosnian reports, perhaps there is photos, but there are also documents generated by you or your colleagues. At least that's what I heard you say. So these documents which were produced by your colleagues in analysing what other documents might have said, these are now in your possession?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these documents are in the video. I hold them in my hands while talking. They are also in my personal file and bear no mark of confidentiality. If you freeze some stills from the video, you will see that. They are the same as the ones I had in my safe. I can send them by post or deliver them otherwise. As for other UNPROFOR reports, I didn't see a single real report with conclusions from the Sarajevo sector. It didn't exist, because nobody wanted the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me, perhaps, look at it from a different angle. When you went to see General Bachelet at the end of your investigation, you were held back by his military assistant. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that's not quite so. He couldn't hold me back, because he was a major and I was a colonel. He said, and I believed him, that there was no chance the report would be accepted with such conclusions, and there was no chance to propagate, publish this information that I arrived at, and I believed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And you can talk about the report. So what did you show to him? What exactly did you show to him, and what did he refer to when he said that's not going to be published? I'm interested in that report as it were.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I brought him that batch of documents that I referred to several times a day, the firing tables, two reports, the Bosnian one and the Dutch one, the drawings, and the one-sentence conclusion, "The Serbs didn't do it." I showed him the documents and I told him so. I told him the Serbs didn't do it, and that was enough for him to respond, "No. No chance. No way."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So there is - apart from one sentence - there is no kind of comprehensive report in Russian or any other language that would kind of be the gist of -- of your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, because it wasn't necessary. It was so obvious that it wasn't necessary to write it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I will come to that I guess later, but since we are on that similar topic, you said that you made a film and you took photographs of the sites you were visiting. Where are these photographs now? Where's the film now?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my personal file at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be -- I can only talk about myself. That would be very important information to -- to relay to us, these photos. And the film? Did you say a film as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't say anything about film. I didn't have a video camera. I had a still camera, not even a digital one, and the -- the photographs are in my personal archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Although I think in your public appearance you said, "I filmed it," but that might have been a translation issue. Anyway, these photos are in your possession in Russia as well. And just to conclude again what your colleagues did, the chief of engineer from the Russian battalion, they didn't produce anything in writing and then submit to you, which you still have in your possession?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of engineering, as I said, collected information on minefields and enabled the group to identify, locate the minefields. And if the location we needed was in a minefield, he would enable us to have access without getting killed. For that you didn't need any documents. It was practical work; that is, to save the lives of the investigation team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Just going back to that encounter with the military assistant of General Bachelet. Do you remember the date? Was it the same day you went public, on the 2nd of September, or was it on the 1st of September that you tried to get to General Bachelet, or was it on another day?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was on the 1st. I'm not quite sure, but it was towards the end of the investigation. That is, it must have been either the 31st of August or the 1st of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you perhaps remember what time of the day it was, and the location?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The location was the next-door office. I didn't have to travel to see General Bachelet. I had to make two steps to the next office. And as for the time of day, I can't tell you. It could have been late at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then when you tried to get to General Bachelet who was next door, you ran into his military assistant, or how come that the military assistant was in between you and your superior?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is standard procedure. If in the anteroom the aide-de-camp or the commander knows there is a meeting upcoming or some documents to be received, it's necessary to first clear it with him. If it's something spontaneous, initiated by a subordinate, you have to see the aide-de-camp and explain why you want to meet the general, what you want to show to him. So it was perfectly normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the aide-de-camp, ADC, or military assistant, he was a Canadian? You said a Canadian?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am 90 per cent certain that he was a Canadian officer, but I may be mistaken. Maybe General Gobillard had a Canadian ADC, but if you really want to be sure, you can go to the G1 part of the archive and find out who the aide-de-camp was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was he perhaps Colonel Fortin, F-o-r-t-i-n? Or Major Fortin at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A colonel could not have been an ADC. It was a duty to be occupied by a major, but as I said, I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where was his office in -- was it in between your office and the office of General Bachelet, or maybe on the other side of the doorway?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to custom we were all in one building. The commander was somewhere along the hallway. But first when you open that door you enter an anteroom, and then through the next door is the office of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Was there anybody else present at the conversation -- or the encounter, rather, between you and the ADC, or was it just you and him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. We were alone, the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how long did that meeting last?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said yesterday that you were in a dilemma between several options. You had, in fact, you said two options, either to stop or to become public. Wasn't there a third option for you, as the chief of staff or alter-ego of the commander, to call him again and get in touch with him before making something you had described as, I think, illegal, or an act of insubordination, whatever your words were? Wouldn't there have been a third way, actually, to try and get in touch with your commander? Maybe wait an hour before making that huge step to -- to get out of the chain of command of UNPROFOR and go public?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're perfectly right. In reality, one has more freedom than one often imagines, but in the life of a military man there are much fewer choices. One reason that did not allow me to take the path you suggest is this: I realised perfectly well that if General Bachelet accepts responsibility, personal responsibility, for that kind of investigation, he will relieve me partially of that responsibility and take it upon himself. And by doing so, he may invite a death sentence upon himself. And the General Bachelet was a man whom I had great respect for and didn't wish him that. And I thought to myself, I'll take the risk on my own. I'm not going to set anyone else up. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can I make a suggestion about scheduling? I'm sure you're aware that I need certainly the whole -- the whole of today with this witness, and since, I think, the feeling is that he needs to come back with his documents and certainly the photos at a later stage, and since he needs to catch a plane later today, I can suggest that I continue for about an hour. I understand that the Defence has another witness which we have not finished yet lined up. So that would be a compromise, but I'm of course in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that's a workable proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before we started this session, Mr. Waespi and I spoke about this problem. I think that we concluded that this witness would need to come back, that Mr. Waespi needs additional time for this witness. I am not allowed to contact the witness regarding this issue because the cross-examination has started, so the witness needs to be explained, and I think that it is up to the Chamber to do this, to explain it to him that he will need to come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the Chamber will do so at an appropriate time. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Going back to the ADC of General Bachelet, do you remember whether that was his standard ADC, or was it somebody who just stood in for the maybe main ADC who was out of town?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember. At any rate, I was supposed to discuss with ADC the issues that I wanted to raise and that's what I did. I just knew that the ADC was there at his duty post.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Another fact I wanted to ask you about is the fact that nowhere in these UN documents, and maybe you have some in -- in Russia, about you conducting an investigation. There is -- or an inquiry or whatever you want to call it. There is talk about, you know, the UNMO investigation. There is talk about the other things going on. And given the fact that you were the releasing officer of quite a number of these official UNPROFOR situation reports, I wonder whether you ever considered in mentioning the fact that you were doing something in one of these UN reports.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the official UNPROFOR documents, strictly speaking I don't know that there are any other documents other than daily, weekly, and monthly assessments, the ones that I signed. And in addition to this, I also wrote standard operating procedures for Sector Sarajevo. I signed them. I don't remember signing any other UNPROFOR documents. Now, as for the investigation, I already spoke to you about that. Had I been ordered, had I been asked, or had I been approached at any level and asked to put it in writing, to put the conclusions that my group and I had reached in writing, I would have done it gladly. However, none of the officials asked me to do that. And this was something that I expected throughout the time that I was there until the end of December. And you have to agree that it was quite strange that nobody asked me to do this, which means that they were not interested in it. Otherwise, they would have asked them -- asked me. And insubordination is not something that is desirable in any armed forces. Initiative is not welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In the course of these three, four days during which you started your investigation, I think you said you started on the 28th of August already. Did you still attend the normal staff meetings during which there would have been an opportunity to raise any of these matters with your commander? When I talk about staff meetings, I mean meetings of your UNPROFOR staff, Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. The regular standard planned activity of the staff went on, including the command staff to which I belonged. However, the issue of that incident was not raised, because practically there was a veto on information concerning that incident. There was an impression that the spokesperson of the UNPROFOR BH command was the only one authorised to publicize the truth, and everybody else had to pretend that they went along with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you did have these meetings. Usually there are morning meetings with senior staff, including yourself and including General Bachelet. I just want to make sure I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. That was the standard procedure. We had our morning meetings. They were not necessarily presided over by General Bachelet. I could not confirm to you that throughout those three days we met with General Bachelet every morning. It's possible that he was absent. However, we continued with our work. There were no interruptions in regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And there was no opportunity for you to kind of tap on the shoulder of General Bachelet, if indeed he was around, and tell him, "You remember, you know, we discussed over the phone a couple of days ago the investigation. You know, now two or three days later, you know, I'm kind of approaching a conclusion"? Wouldn't there be a way for you to communicate with your -- your superior?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely that would have been the case. However, it's always much easier to make such claims in hindsight. I didn't really look for a possibility to approach General Bachelet with this. He consented to me doing this work, and I did this work. I did not consider it necessary to further get him involved in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: After the incident or whatever, did you ever have a chance to discuss with General Bachelet that, or you -- when you left UNPROFOR there was no more contact with you with anybody from UNPROFOR, including General Bachelet?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite follow you. As I have already explained to you, on the 28th in the evening I met with General Bachelet. We discussed this incident briefly. Both of us reached the conclusion that it was a terrible tragic event, probably the most tragic event, during our stay there in 1995. We both concluded that on one side we had to make sure that our soldiers were safe, and on the other hand we had to become more active in monitoring the activities of the warring sides. On my part I suggested to him that I could head the investigation group. That was what we discussed. And further we did not discuss this issue for the reasons I explained earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And then we have your attempt to talk to him on the 1st or 2nd September, and my question is did you at any time later, you know, in September, in October, in December of 1995, or maybe even in 1996, or 1997, 2000, discuss your findings, your conclusions, your report, your suspicion, with General Bachelet?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. Naturally I had a conversation with General Bachelet several days after the interview -- a day or two after the interview. He looked quite distressed, and the reasons for that were quite understandable. As I have already explained to you information was leaked that to a certain extent discredited him, General Rupert Smith, maybe somebody else above them, and it simply slipped out of his control. And humanly speaking, I fully sympathised with him. I understood it. I sympathised with him and everybody else whom I got in trouble without wanting to do that. But let me say once again that to take up the initiative and to say, "Let me write, let me tell, let me explain," was something that there was no need for me to do because nobody asked me to do that. I said that I was ready to announce the truth, and UNPROFOR said, "We will send you back to Russia." That was the end of the discussion. There was no need for me to explain anything else. After that, I was sent to Mons to NATO staff there to head the Russian section at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a final point. When you talked to the ADC, did you -- I think you already explained, and I'm sorry for going back to that, that showed him, you know, your documents. Do you remember having shown him the photos as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the photographs had already been developed. I showed him the photographs, firing tables, various papers, and I told him what our conclusion was. Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the last point on this issue, did you have any contacts with the VRS, with the army of the Republika Srpska, or with any other representative of the Republika Srpska during those days, you know, on -- after the explosion on the 28th of August? Did you talk with any of -- of these people? Of course about the events.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have contact. The routine regime went on. A liaison officer, Indjic, who was an officer of the SRK, was constantly in touch with UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo. Routinely I would meet both with liaison officer of the VRS army and the BH army. I think the liaison officer for the BH army was Colonel Lugonja or something like that. I did not discuss our report with him because it had nothing to do with Republika Srpska. It had -- it only concerned me and the people that I was responsible to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But did you give them a sense of what you were doing, that you were doing kind of a side investigation to the official UNPROFOR investigations? Were they aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they knew about it or not. If they followed me, if they had me under surveillance then, yes, they probably would have known because I was in their territory. I was in the territory of one of the warring sides. So it's probable that they knew about it. But I didn't find it necessary to deliberately inform them about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about that now, the trips you made. Who went to see these potential firing positions of mortars? Was it of you, was you and your driver/bodyguard? Was there somebody else? Can you tell us a little bit more about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And on how many days did you do that, or just on one day?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. You mean visiting the site of the incident or visiting firing positions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, the latter. You talked in your TV appearance that you went through these rocky areas and determined it was impossible to fire a 120-millimetre mortar from the places you've seeing, that part of your investigation. When did you go?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand now. There were always several of us going on those tours. As I said, Captain Tyulenev, then artillery men from the Russian battalion. It is quite possible somebody else joined us. So there was a always a number of us. The principal was quite simple. We were look to at the fire tables and coordinate in order to establish with a margin of error of one to two metres the exact location. Unfortunately, at the time we didn't not have a GPS device, but we were able to use the traditional old fashioned instruments to determine the location. I would stand at the location and they would take a make photograph of me in order to establish that within the radius that would roughly be that of this room. It was impossible to fire from that location because there was a forest there in one location. And on the other location there was a pristine meadow, and it would have been impossible to fire from there either. And then in the third location there were just too many rocks and boulders, and again it would have been impossible to place a weapon there. Those are the locations that we visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let's take it step-by-step. You personally -- did I understand you correctly, you personally with your driver/bodyguard visited four locations, the four locations you pointed out in that video we've seen yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's the only location you personally visited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Robinson, the question put to this witness was, "You toured these locations just with your driver escorting you," but that's not the case. The witness explained there was always a number of them, and he even mentioned ranks of the people who accompanied -- accompanied him on those locations. It wasn't just him and the driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's for the witness to -- to correct that. I think the counsel was putting it to him. Or were you putting it to him that he -- as something that he had already said in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I'm aware that there was a team. And in fact that's what I'm trying to figure out, which locations the witness himself visited and if there were other locations that other members of his team visited. I'm just not entirely clear at this stage about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, Colonel, you yourself and your driver visited these four locations? That's number one.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. It's not that I just visited and photographed these locations with a still camera. We didn't film them. We photographed them with a still camera. And if you remember, there was also the fifth location that we showed in the video, because one of the observers pointed to this possible fifth location, and we did visit it too. Naturally, we thoroughly visited it wherever the minefields allowed. We visited dozens of locations, physically visited them and investigated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just following on your last answer. What dozens of locations did you visit? So you not only visited these four locations you identified and pointed out during your presentation, you also visited dozens of locations.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We visited them. We travelled there in APCs and then continued on foot. So we would get to a certain point that we calculated on the basis of the angle of descent, and then we would go on foot, either climb or descend, and it was probably thousands of metres that we walked on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just to make sure that I understand that, was it the whole group that would be always together, or was it just you and your driver to visit some locations and your colleagues would visit other locations, or is it a combination, that sometimes you would be alone with your driver and sometimes you would split up? Can you explain the mechanics of your trip?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly can. However, I don't think that the Chamber would be interested in technical details. This is what it looked like: First we did theoretical work on the basis of documents. We drew a line on the map. Following that, we sent officers, engineers, who conducted reconnaissance of minefields and either made a passage through minefields or were able to establish that there were no minefields there. Thus there was no danger for us. Then other officers would mark with cones the line so that we could easily follow the line. In addition that, artillery specialists would visit the location and mark on the spot, the very spot from which this shell was allegedly fired. So everybody did their job. I went with the captain and the man who made photographs, who was also an officer. We moved along that line, and we photographed all the possible spots from which the shell could have been fired. It's a thorough, detailed, laborious type of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But I'm -- I just want to go back to my earlier point. Did other people from your group, like these artillery specialists, did they visit locations you did not visit yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood you. The entire area of responsibility covered by the Russian battalion had to be very well-known to them, and they had to be there. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm just asking whether you personally visited all the spots you thought were potential firing spots according to what you heard analysed in these reports? You personally did that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did that myself, and I have on record photographs which show me pointing my finger on the location, and the photographs corroborate the -- the argument that I'm making.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that you drew a line on the map which would be sort of the guiding principle for you to visit these locations and that line, I guess, would be what you knew from the reports was the possible direction of fire, that was 176 degrees. That's at least what you said in this public appearance.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two numbers, at least two numbers there. One referring to the bearings, the azimuth, and when degrees are mentioned it's the angle of descent. I believe it was 67 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And the direction of fire if you take a 360 degree circle, I know -- I think the NATO count was 6.400 mils., and I think the Russian army 6.000. These are all ways to calculate the direction of fire. But looking at the 360 degree circle of a watch, of a clock, you would look at a possible direction of fire of 176 degrees?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. And what you did, and you explained it nicely on that chart behind you, is you followed this or looked at these four possible locations which were on the Bosnian Serb side which correspond to the possible charges used to fire that shell, namely charge three, four, five, and six.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And so the guiding principle for you to look at these locations was this line of 176 degrees.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the line and the angle. The angle indicated the exact locations of fire points.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, because looking at the JNA charts, you were able to calculate at what distance a specific charge would be fired achieving this angle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
