utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if we could have a map, 03346A, please. This is a map, Colonel, which hopefully depicts the area of where you were venturing out on -- on those days. And while that's being retrieved, can I ask you again, did you visit these four locations on one day or was it spread over several days?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was spread over two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And which two days would that be?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th, we did the theory work, the calculations using firing tables and maps. On the 30th we were on location, and possibly on the 31st we continued working on the location. Two, two and a half days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And starting on the 30th, what time in the morning did you leave?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will understand that 12 years later it's difficult -- it's difficult to remember the chronology of the site visits, but we tried to set out early in the morning and work until dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate your answer. I agree it's difficult to cast your mind back such a long time and talk about details. Do you see a map in front of you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you orient yourself on this map?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you see the Old Town of -- of Sarajevo, especially the dark brown part which delineates the area where Markale was, just in a general sense?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And obviously if you looked at a direction of fire of 170 degrees, which is almost half of the circle, and if you look at a watch it's 6.00, so you would have looked at all these locations, you know, in the south of the city. Now, can you take a pen and just -- we can even enlarge the photo, and if --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can you help the Witness, please? There is no need to rush.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And really take your time, and your markings need to be clear, and you have made such a nice chart, and we saw from your TV presentation 12 years ago that you're a capable presenter. So take your time and please show us the way, the exact way you travelled, perhaps even indicating where you travelled by car. You said you used an APC. And then where you left the car and where you walked on foot. And perhaps just think about it first, orient yourself, and then as clear and as precise as you're able to, tell us which location you visited on the 30th of August and perhaps even the next day. And I'm only interested now in this part, looking at the degree of 176, and not the other one, which I think was about 230 degrees near Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what is the scale of this map, because I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just look at the original, please. Now it's slightly distorted also because we have enlarged it. Unfortunately it says on my map scale "not available," but we do have a similar map, a street map, which has a scale, and perhaps you can compare those two with each other, which allows you to be correct. We can do that. We can give you 28 -- this is ter number 2872. That's a normal commercial street map. And perhaps you want to look at that first. So since you didn't make a marking that, I think we can leave that the way it is and go back to the street map and that has a scale. It indicates what a thousand metres is. Yes. The map we are looking at has a scale of 1:20.000. That's the next one we will see in a moment. And I appreciate your comment about the scale. That's a very important issue before you mark any map. Thanks. Thanks for that. Yes, Colonel, this is a commercial map, and the scale, as I said, is 1:20.000, and at the bottom to the right you see a little marking, legend. That's what 1 kilometre is.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what am I supposed to do, show it on this map or on the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You can do it on this one, if you prefer. And since we are talking about that, let's do it on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the area south of the Old Town could be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just feel obliged to say, since this is a scale of 1:20.000, that military maps are always on a scale of 1:25.000, 1:50.000 or 1:100.000, but a military map can never be 1:20.000. For a military expert of this profile to give us some information. This is a commercial street map as my colleague Mr. Waespi said himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can just offer two maps. I can offer the first one, and I'll inquire what the scale was, but this one gives you a rough idea about the distances so you can acquaint yourselves about the distances, and I think we could go back to the first happen. It's up to you, whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, it's all the same to me. You understand this is a, frankly speaking, prehistoric, obsolete method, very primitive. What can I do here? I can draw an approximate line, but that cannot be the real thing. You cannot hold me to that. I can take a military map and the material from that video presentation, and then with a proper map I can draw a proper line. That will take only 10 minutes of an IT specialist's time. On this map I can approximately indicate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not interested in the line, I'm interested in the locations you visited and even more, in the way, the actual route that you took on the 28th. And I would feel more comfortable, Colonel, if we would go back to the first map that we talked about, but only if you feel comfortable as well.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any map would be good.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the first map, because it's more detailed and it has the contour lines. And the number of that map was 03346A. Yes. And it's obviously a military map as well, because it shows the -- some parts of the warring factions. Yes. I think that's a good cutout right now. Don't go any further. Yes. You need to go more to the -- the cutout has to be bigger. It was perfect just a moment ago. More to the -- yes. I think that's fine. That should be it. That should be okay, yes. So can you indicate, and really take your time, the route you took on the 28th -- on the -- I think you said on the 30th of August, and perhaps the next day, in discovering possible mortar locations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm mostly interested less in -- in these calculated drawings than the actual route. What did you do -- where did you start? When you came from Sarajevo, which route did you take? Where did you leave the APC and start to work on foot as you told us a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you look at this drawing, approximately, and I underline approximately, you see the route of the APC. Usually I would set out in my car from Sarajevo to Grbavica, to the Russian battalion. There we would switch to an APC. We moved along roughly this route up to a point where you see a little circle, and from there on we went on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just take it step-by-step. It's really important, Colonel, that we get an idea of your actual route you took. You said you had an APC, and you say that from a certain point. "Where there is a little circle from there we went on foot." Please mark that point from where you went on foot with the letter A.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So -- and I'm just trying to find out how you reached that point. Did you follow from Grbavica the route towards Pale, then crossed this imaginary line, which is your blue line, to the village of Knjegnjac, and then you took that turned road towards your letter A? Was that the route you took?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either that, or we followed the blue line that you see through the fields. The track. Not the real road but the dirt track. We used all possibilities. An APC can overcome a slope of 30 degrees, so it was an all terrain thing. It could handing that terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let me put it differently. Which of these four locations, the possible firing locations of a mortar, did you visit first, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, we started from the front end, this point that I'm showing now, this little cross that I'm putting now, on the confrontation line practically. That was the beginning. And then we went down from point to point along this route on the front line side into the depth that is behind the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Let's start with location number one. Can you put -- I know which one you mean, the one at the confrontation lines, but please put the number 1 beside it. The first location you visited?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Great?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, could I suggest that we coordinate with the drawing made already by the witness so that we would call that C3, and then C4 and C5 and C6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's an excellent suggestion, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, how did you get to location number as 3 as it is now? Previously 1. It's now 3. You went by APC. Where did you leave it, and where did you walk towards?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reached every point by walking. We would leave our APC in any convenient place that was safe, outside of minefields, not under fire by either warring party. I cannot show you on the map because there were dozens of such locations. I can improvise, of course, but I don't think this is the proper place for improvising.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So in relation to the first location, location 3, you remember what you saw there? What kind of area was it? If you recall after such a long time, and perhaps the map and the contours, it's green - it appears to be wooded - reminds you of that. Can you explain us what you saw there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I remember all the four points perfectly well, but which one of them corresponds to which site on the map I can not tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have a hard copy --

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have photographs, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I have a hard copy of the same location, so -- which is not touched by your markings, which kind of covers some, perhaps, even important information contained on the maps like contours. So I think it might be easier for you to look at the untouched map, and at the same time we can continue working on your interactive map as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if the witness could be shown -- you can show it to counsel as well. In fact, counsel can have a map as well. And if Your Honours would like to see a hard copy, I'm certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I'm going to ask you to stop at about 7 minutes to 11.00 so that I can make the arrangements for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honours -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So just talking about this first location, number 3, just tell us as much as you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm the only one, it seems, who didn't get the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic has not received a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map disappeared from my screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, Witness, just tell us as much as you can about this location which is now number 3. What do you remember? How far away from the road, this transit road Pale-Lukavica it was? I know it's a long time ago and it's kind of perhaps even guesswork, but just try to help us a little bit about how you reached that location. Were there minefields to cross through? Did you meet people, soldiers from any warring factions at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's perfectly obvious that we passed through the front line of the Army of the Republika Srpska. The Defence positions were standard. We didn't see anything out of the ordinary there. The troops were on duty. We were led through by a local commander who would show us that there was no minefield there, that it was safe. And we reached our destination point without running any risks; although, the exchange of firing between two warring sides continued. It was on a slope approximately one kilometre from the road leading east, and there's not much to add, as you must know. These maps tend to become obsolete after a while. Although I see that this is dated 2007, the surveys underlying the map were done 10 or even 20 years before. So there could be a field or a dirt track through. Our standard procedure would be to run through the reference points indicated by the artillery men, make sure that it was possible to photograph, make photographs, make sure that the reference point was not going to come under fire, and then we would move further into the rear towards point number 4. You see these are very difficult slopes at a very large angle, which in itself tells you that it's impossible to place a mortar there. The fields were flat completely like a golf terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How long did it take you, as far as you remember, from the location where you left the APC, then talking to this local commander who accompanied you to the suspected fire location? How long did all that action take, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It was not a problem. The entire distance was five kilometres. If you multiply it by the gradient, we took two days all in all, two and a half days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sorry, can I interrupt you Witness? I'm really only focusing on this location which is now marked as 3. You told us just a moment ago that you were met by a local commander. There were a few minefields, and you went to the suspected location. How long did that action last on that first suspected fire location number 3? How long it take for you to go there to take the photo, to interact with these soldiers? Can you tell us after such a long time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember. I personally didn't talk to any soldiers. The UNPROFOR doesn't look kindly upon that sort of thing. The local officer had to make sure that we were not fired upon, mistaking us for the enemy, but I was not the one who contacted with the local commander. He was told to assist us by the higher command. And there were no minefields, thank God. It took approximately two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Hold your fire. There are some logistical matters that we have to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are considering how to get the documents to the witness. It has been said that some of them are confidential and that the better course might be to have the witness come back at least a day before so that he could prepare, but another option would be to lift the confidentiality so that the witness can prepare himself properly. He is of course not to discuss his evidence with anybody, and I will tell him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. He could photocopy maybe the cover page of each document and send it by e-mail or fax to court officers who could then ask for UN clearance, because that's a very, very quick process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I'm now talking about the documents that we have. We would lift the confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. As I say, I don't think any of these documents are confidential any more. I think there might be one or two sketches which were under seal, but that only concerned because the witness was a protected witness. In my view all these documents are public documents which can be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes and if any is confidential, we will take the necessary steps to lift that confidentiality. So that by Monday we would have a collection of all the documents to be sent to the witness. Now, as far as the witness is concerned: Witness, the documents that you have and which may need translation, we would have to arrange for you to send them to the Tribunal so that they can be translated. Another matter to consider is the timing. We have about three and a half weeks left in this term, and then when we resume, in principal only we only have one week in August. So it would seem to me that the arrangement should be made for the witness to return prior to the 26th of July. That would be the best arrangement. So, Witness, this is what is going to happen: The Registrar or the Victims and Witnesses Unit is going to contact you as to when you should return. You are not to discuss the -- your evidence with anybody. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will have the documents sent to you so that you can read them and be prepared for your testimony when you return. In relation to the documents that you have and that need to be translated, arrangements will be made for you to send those documents to the Tribunal well ahead of time so that they can be translated. Is there anything else, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. For us, I think the photos would be equally important so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. He's to bring -- when I say documents, I include in that the photographs that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I do have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to clarify something. I told you that the documents that were part of investigation that I held in my hands in the video are not confidential, and I could either mail them or send them via courier to you. As for the documents that are marked as confidential, those are just ordinary reports concerning firing incidents, and they can be found in UNPROFOR archives. For me they represented a memento, and as for whether the Court would accept them as documentary evidence, that is quite a different matter. That is something that did not arise in our work. Do you really need these firing incident reports as part of documentary evidence here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To the extent that they are relevant, yes, we will need them. So bring all of them. The confidentiality can't stand in the way of the progress of the case. If there is a procedure that is to be followed in relation to documents that are UN documents and are confidential, then we'll follow it, but the court proceedings take precedence over that confidentiality. So we will make contact with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question, a minor one. Could it please be done in such a way as to accommodate my schedule? I'm quite a busy man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent that that is possible, of course. Do you have particular dates? Can you identify now dates that -- when you would be available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have dates for which I have other engagements scheduled. I'm director of a plant, and I'm quite busy. I'm fully busy between the 19th and the 25th of July, and then from the 2nd to the 5th of August. Right now I'm available at other times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that will be taken into account, and the Registrar will make the appropriate arrangements. It would seem then that an effort should be made to have you here before the -- before the 19th, before the 19th, but we'll take that into account. And remember, you're not to discuss your evidence with anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may now leave, and you will be advised when you are to return. It's 11.00. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is the last item. I don't mind if the witness wants to take that map with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which one, the one on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may take that. Yes, he may take that map with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if the video could be saved -- the map on the screen could be saved as well and tendered as an exhibit for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as P807, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So my understanding now, Mr. Tapuskovic, is that we would return to the witness who was giving evidence two days ago. That is whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Rade Ivanovic. D-22 -- or T-22. Cross-examination was in progress when we interrupted his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Cross-examination. That's Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just have your indulgence for a moment so that I could log on to the transcript on LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Whenever you're ready to begin, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Ivanovic. I'd like to resume --

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to resume what we had begun two days ago in asking you questions based on your examination-in-chief and some other matters, and to go back to something that you said when you and I were talking two days ago. You confirmed that you had been a member of the Crisis Staff for the Serbian municipality of Trnovo from 21 April 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you confirmed that Radivoje Draskovic who was the SDS president for Trnovo, and you thought that as head of the party he also held the position as head of the Crisis Staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, apart from you and Draskovic, who else was on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Trnovo battalion Danilo Golijanin, and several other members whose names I cannot recall right now. I believe one was -- one was Danilo Golijanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I asked you a couple of times whether you would agree with me that the purpose of the Crisis Staff was to organise the Serbs dealing with both civilian and military issues, and you replied focusing on two things, that as the police you dealt with mostly civilian matters, and that the main purpose of the Crisis Staff, you said, was to protect the population from possible conflicts and attacks. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the civilian police was to protect the civilian population. The Crisis Staff was also supposed to work on behalf of the civilian population in order to protect them from certain unfavourable situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in that context, and at the time you were a member of the Crisis Staff for Trnovo, had very much a military role or function, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, as well as in May, it had no military function.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right, then. With that answer I'd like to ask for document 03365 to be brought up on the screen for us. Now, these documents, Mr. Ivanovic, are minutes of the meeting of the SDS Crisis Staff for Trnovo, dated 29 April, 1992. Now, just looking at the list of meeting attendees at the top of the document, you would agree with me that you were present at this meeting. Isn't that correct? It you have trouble reading it, you can say and Mr. President registrar might be able to enlarge the list of meeting attendees for you. Do you see your name on the first line -- last name on the first line of the meeting attendees?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, along with you, Draskovic, Golijanin, I see the names also a Glisa Simonic; Nedjo Vlaski; Andjelko Milic, who you named previously; Savo Vlacic; Dragan Klepic; Radmilo Golijanin. These were all members of the Crisis Staff with you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedjo Vlaski did attend the meetings of the Crisis Staff although he was not a member. As for the others listed, I think all of them were members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn to another page in this document with the B/C/S document. It's the last paragraph. If you could scroll down. I hope I have this correct. On the bottom of page 1 that you see in front of you. And this same entry should appear on English page 2. Do you see, Mr. Ivanovic, where Radivoje Draskovic begins speaking, the last paragraph on the bottom of page 1, he reports there on his meeting with the JNA and says: "We agreed with the JNA representatives, and they will get involved in," and he uses the words "cicenje opstine." We have to get crews for APCs and tanks. This is good because of the psychological moment. The army is ready to clear up the situation in Trnovo." That's what he's recorded as saying at the meeting at which you were present, Mr. Ivanovic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now I cannot remember whether things went exactly as this. There was some discussion about the protection of the Serbian people, because in Sarajevo as of April 4 there were combat activities in certain locations in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And actually, that doesn't answer my question, does it, Mr. Ivanovic, because I asked you -- I read to you the paragraph and simply asked you whether that -- what I've read to you is accurately reflected in the minutes that you've read. Is what I read to you accurately reflected in the document in front of you in?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I no longer see what Radivoje Draskovic said. I see the last paragraph only. It seems that there are three portions of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go back, please. If we could go back to page 1, please, bottom of page 1 of the B/C/S copy. You see Radivoje Draskovic in the very second sentence reports on his meeting with the JNA, saying: "We've agreed with the JNA representatives, and they will get involved in ciscenje opstine." Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly right now. I suppose this is correct since it is a part of the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wasn't certain, Your Honours, if the correct English portion of the document was appearing on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and the words that you read in B/C/S mean mopping up or cleaning -- or cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I see beside it "unclear." Why is "unclear" written beside it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't speak to whoever made the translation of this document, so I simply reverted to the words as they appeared in the B/C/S document to rely on my colleagues in the interpretation booth to give the correct interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, have we had that? May I ask the interpreter what is the correct interpretation of -- I will not dare to try to pronounce it, but you know the two words that we are speaking of, ciscenje opstine.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is very difficult to conclude based on the context itself. It remains ambiguous. Either of the two options offered might be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the two options are what, mopping up or cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, looking at this document and seeing what the president of the Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the problem is the word itself, ciscenje. Except for the phrase ciscenje opstine, there is nothing else in that sentence. The word ciscenje is stripped bear. There is no qualification assigned to it within that sentence. There is something else that I cannot read which was handwritten. However, the word ciscenje remains completely isolated. There is nothing to explain it. Whether it pertains to any type of cleaning, I really don't know. There is nothing else but that one word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's your submission then? Are you asking us to do anything about it or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that my learned friend, Madam Prosecutor, should try and expand on that, should try and ask the witness to give an interpretation of it. I don't think I am allowed to do that. Perhaps the Prosecutor has an interpretation of her own and maybe we could hear something from the witness as well. If we are going to consider this word "ciscenje," I believe my learned friend should follow up on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In terms of the purpose that this particular evidence is designed to serve, it doesn't appear to the Trial Chamber that it matters much. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So my question to you now, Mr. Ivanovic, is wouldn't you agree with me that the Crisis Staff -- according this document the Crisis Staff for the Serbian municipality of Trnovo, of which you were a member, was involving the JNA in the ciscenje of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA did not take part in any activities in April Trnovo at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is cross-examination, I expect my learned friend to put to the witness exactly what this cleaning or cleansing was about. She can put to him whether this was cleansing of people, cleaning of streets. There is nothing else here except for the word "ciscenje." If my learned friend wants to suggest anything to the witness I won't object. Why insist on the word "cicenje" any further when there is nothing there to explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But she has put to him that the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Trnovo, of which he was a member, was involved with the JNA in the ciscenje, which is the cleaning of the municipality. You would want her to go further and to put to the witness what the cleaning was about. Was it a cleansing of people or a cleansing of anything else. Well, that depends on whether the witness agrees with the proposition. Do you agree then, Witness, having seen the document that the Crisis Staff was involving the JNA in the ciscenje of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just tried to tell you that the JNA took no part in any activities in Trnovo in April. There were some reservists there of the VRS, as well as the local population and the local Serb police. Other than that, there was no one else there in April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the date of this document, Ms. Edgerton? Can we see the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 29 April 1992, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 29th April. I see. And the witness's position is that the JNA took no part in any activities in Trnovo in April, and you would maintain that position notwithstanding the -- what you have seen in the document. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am sure that the JNA took no part in any activities in Trnovo in April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On that note, we will take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, I have one more question about this same document and the same paragraph. I'd like you to -- I'd like to direct you to the sentence immediately after the one we were talking about. If you could find it again at the bottom of the page. It says: "We have to provide an area for military personnel carriers and tanks." Or, actually, "We have to provide terrain for military personnel, carriers and tanks." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Isn't this a military function, providing an area for military personnel carriers and tanks?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, in April there was no JNA in Trnovo. Once I got through the entire minutes now, I realised that this was a preparatory meeting since there was a danger for the Serb people in Trnovo since they were in the minority. There were only 28 per cent Serbs in Trnovo. This was a preparation meeting aimed at gaining assistance from the part of the army that was in Kalinovik according to the words of Radivoje Draskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Therefore, then, the Crisis Staff was engaging in military functions at that time, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April there were no military functions in Trnovo. The only thing that went on were the preparations for the defence of the Serb people against potential attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Your Honours, I'd like to have this document entered, please, as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P808, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I move on to one further document, ter number 03371, please. 03371 minutes of the Crisis Staff meeting for the Serbian municipality, dated 18 May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see your name among the attendees at the top of the page, Mr. Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could move, please, to page 2 in both versions of the document. One, two, three -- fourth paragraph of the English where Mr. Glisa Simonic is speaking, and in page 2 of the B/C/S. First paragraph of the document. There, Mr. Ivanovic, Glisa says, "We at the Command and Crisis Staff should be as," one and Draskovic responds, "There is no drastic peace without ethnically clean territories." Simonic mentions meetings with the Minister of the Interior Kosorac and Gagovic, and then continues: "You cannot free a town without destroying it with artillery and conquering it with infantry." Do you see all that on the page before you, sir? It's underlined, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Have you found the portion I've read to you, sir? Do you have trouble finding it, sir? Should I direct you to it on the page?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to read the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you found the portion that says: "You cannot free a town without destroying it with artillery and conquering it with infantry," sir?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, about two weeks after this Crisis Staff meeting took place, that's exactly what happened in Trnovo municipality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what you have in mind. I know what happened two weeks after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Around 29 or 30 May, Serb residents started evacuating Trnovo, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th of May --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the Serb population --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- left Trnovo, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. On 29 May, Colonel Ratko Bundalo told Zeljko Spasojevic, and you know who he is, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you have in mind, Zeljko Spasojevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Zeljko Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know I him. He's the man from Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel Bundalo told him there would be attack on Trnovo and the Muslims would be driven out. That's exactly what happened, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th of May we, the civilian police, were in the culture hall in the settlement of Trnovo itself. We functioned as a police station there. We left that station because it had been agreed that the civilians would be evacuated because it was announced that the Muslim forces would attack Trnovo. Therefore, the civilians left Trnovo and moved to the village of Tosce, which is in the vicinity some three kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, we're talking about the Serbs now, and we've already dealt with the Serb evacuation of it Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On the 31st of May, Serb forces shelled Trnovo for several hours, didn't they, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And following that non-Serbs evacuated Trnovo in large numbers. In fact, there was a total evacuation of non-Serbs from Trnovo, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska entered Trnovo on the 31st of May, and they mostly found Trnovo without any residents in it. Even the Muslim population had left Trnovo. I don't know when they did it, whether they did it in the course of the day or earlier. I couldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I move on to another area, could I have this document entered as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P809, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ivanovic, if I told you that a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal in September 2006 found, among other things, that approximately 2.500 non-Serbs left Trnovo as a result of this attack, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree when it comes to 2.600 residents, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What number would you put it at then, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you an accurate number. I know that in the town of Trnovo the dominant ethnic group among the population was Serbs in town itself, and in the neighbouring villages which were under the control of the Muslim army, the dominant population, was the Muslim one. In the city itself it was the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, moving on to another area, sir, just before we broke on Wednesday I was asking you if it was correct that the Serb people in Trnovo had formed their own TO command. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind, the TO command. The Serbs had organised themselves in order to defend themselves. This was the reserve force of the TO. They were not professional soldiers. This is how it was until late May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At the beginning of the session, as we were coming into court, the court deputy looked at me very sternly and said Ms. Edgerton has 20 minutes left. He pays more attention to those matters than I do. I don't want this witness to have to return. And, Mr. Tapuskovic, you will have re-examination? You may not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Maybe not. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I cannot know that in advance until the cross-examination is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So how much more time will you spend?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, I put it to you that a command for the defence of the Serbian people in Trnovo was established right after the barricades of March 1992, and it was established with Golijanin, yourself, and Zeljko Spasojevic, among others. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, that is not correct. At least my name should not be included there. It was only in April that I was appointed chief of Serbian police. Prior to that I was in the multi-ethnic police, which included Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And are you saying by your answer, sir, that following April 1992 you were a member of the battalion command, the Trnovo battalion command?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not a member of the battalion command. I was chief of civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I please have a document, 03369, brought up on the screen. And the next page, please, of the B/C/S. I'm sorry, I don't know what that is in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to direct you now to a collection of transcripts of Trnovo battalion command meetings going first to page 7 of the B/C/S and the English page 7. Sir, on this page that you see in front of you, this page records a meeting of the Trnovo battalion command of 19 May 1992, and lists you among the participants. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was normally invited to meetings as chief of police, but I was not a member of the command, because the civilian police was separate from the military command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then, sir, even though this collection records you present at battalion command meetings on May 20th, two times on May 22nd, on May 23rd, May 25th, May 27th, May 28th, you assert that you weren't an effective part of the Trnovo battalion command? And I'm not asking about a formal part but an effective part.

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear what your question means. I told you in so many words that I was invited to meetings to brief them as chief as police on the situation in town, but I was not a member of that command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, you appeared and took part in and reported to the Crisis Staff for the Serbian municipality of Trnovo throughout April and May 1992, I put it to you. Throughout May 1992 you were a regular participant in Trnovo battalion command meetings, and I put it to you, sir, that you were involved in every stage of the planning, preparation and participation ultimately in the takeover -- the military takeover of Trnovo municipality, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I have this document tendered as the next exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P810, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now to move on to I think -- to move on to another area, sir. In your previous testimony you said that in November and December 1994, you were made part of the VRS. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember saying to Mr. Tapuskovic that in November and December 1994 you were made part of the VRS? To be more precise, as I recall, you said your elements of your police unit were made part of the VRS. And it was at page 70 of your previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not state it that way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic is going to tell us how it was stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness started answering, so I give up. I don't want to interrupt him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1994, for the month of December, as you stated, Madam Prosecutor, the civilian police was not part of the VRS, the army of Republika Srpska. It assisted ad hoc when defence lines were in jeopardy. In those cases the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska would pass down orders that the civilian police should help out the army, but the police was not part of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May I have document number 03378 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that document, ask you, Mr. Ivanovic, actually this subordination to the VRS, if I can call it that, took place much earlier, didn't it, by 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he never said that they were subordinated to the army of Republika Srpska. He testified that on some occasions when assistance was required the police would join the army of Republika Srpska, would act jointly with the army. That's how it can be stated to the witness, and then he can clarify and provide additional information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That may be an overstatement, Ms. Edgerton. A reformulation then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just move forward by abandoning that and directing the witness to the document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just abandon that formulation and direct the witness to the document that appears on the screen on his right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, can you see that document? Sir? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And isn't it correct that in 1993, in fact August 1993, by order of the VRS Main Staff and on direction of the SRK commander at that time, General Galic, you and seven others were moved from the MUP Ilidza to the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade with a view to establishing the Trnovo battalion?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at this document but I was not a part of the army. I was not a member of the army. I know that Aleksa Ivanovic was not a member the army either. And I was not in the Ilidza MUP as I said before. I was working at the police station of Kula. I don't know the other persons here. I don't know Srdjan Veletic or the others. I know about the first one, Marinko Avramovic, but he was in the police at Ilidza the whole time until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he never transferred to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, are you saying this document doesn't refer to you?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it refers to me, but I never received this order. I never held it in my hands, and I was never transferred.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you have never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you've near seen it before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you were never directed -- whether or not you've seen this order, you were never directed to join with units of the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade in any kind of operations?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. May I explain? Until the end of the war I was on the police force, and later on in peacetime I continued working until end 1999. I have all the documents confirming that I was retired as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, if you weren't given your area of operations or the area on which you purported or said that you were operating in, if you weren't operationally subordinated to the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, who were you subordinated to then?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior, Republika Srpska, specifically to the centre of public security of Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, now, am I correct in my understanding of an operation that when you're called upon by the VRS to come and join them at weak areas of the lines, you don't march in there as an independent unit or independent individuals of the Serbian MUP, you're operationally subordinated to the military command responsible for the area in which you're active. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. When we acted under the command of the army, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, sir, what brigade were you then operationally subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Sarajevo Brigade, I believe. It held the defence positions in the territory of Trnovo municipality in 1993, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to another area that you touched upon in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I won't seek to tender this document in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic. No longer insisting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I just wanted to say that I object to the admission of this document because it isn't signed. I didn't know that it was not going to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just want to move on, sir, to a couple more areas, one being that when you testified in chief about the time you were at the Kula police outpost, you said that: "During the period 1994/1995, there were arrested or detained members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina held in the Kula prison. It wasn't such a large number of them but there were some, and I know that most of them were very quickly exchanged then." Now, sir, do I take from that that you never -- you're asserting you never saw civilians imprisoned at the Kula prison facility?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which civilians do you mean, Madam Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think it was an easy enough question. Were there not civilians imprisoned at Kula along with these members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any civilians in 1993, 1994, 1995 in Kula. I never saw civilians imprisoned at Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that Serb authorities themselves noted that approximately 10.000 -- 10.000 Muslims of all ages had passed through Kula prison up until the period of 28 October 1994. Knowing that -- knowing that, do you still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am not objecting to the question itself, but I would like to know on the basis of what documents is it asserted that 10.000 civilians passed through the prison at Kula? On what grounds? Is it just an offhand number? I think I owe you an explanation, Your Honours, from a few days ago when you used me -- when I used a number and you told me it was not appropriate for anyone, including me, and I owe you a response when you tell me you want me -- you want it. But I do agree that whenever we use numbers we should be careful and precise. Now we hear the number of 10.000 civilians who passed through the prison at Kula. On what basis? The Prosecution should clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Quite apart from that, Ms. Edgerton, I don't consider that you have acted properly in putting the question in that way, because you are putting it to the witness that Serb authorities noted that approximately 10.000 Muslims passed through Kula prison, and then you say, "Knowing that," but the witness has not acknowledged that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May I rephrase, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I can do it certainly by reference to a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So much the better.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I'll reference two sources, the first being document 03389.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, on the screen in front of you is a document dated 28 October 1994, which is a request for assistance addressed to the RS refugee commissariat and the Prime Minister, noting that since the beginning of the war KP Dom Butmir has been a transit point for Muslim civilians going to Sarajevo or other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina in addition to its basic function. The document also notes as you go further that a rough estimate is that 10.000 Muslims of all ages pass through the prison for a few days or a few months. As -- it says further: "As the prison used as a transit point for receipt of Muslim civilians even now," in October 1994, "and will be in the future, it is hoped that a positive answer will be given to secure the basic resources for KP Dom Butmir so that the process of family reunion and freedom of movement for the Muslim population of the RS on the territory of former Bosnia and Herzegovina can continue to be implemented without hindrance." Sir, seeing this correspondence, are you -- do you then still hold to the view that -- the view you expressed during your testimony in chief and recently that there were no civilians incarcerated at Kula?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document there is absolutely no reference to any imprisonment of these people in Kula. It says that only transit was made possible through this institution towards the Muslim part of Sarajevo with the aid of humanitarian organisations. There is no mention of the word "imprisoned" or "imprisonment." And I have that much understanding of this language. It says only that there was transit pending transfer to the Muslim part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, your time has passed, but in any event, point me to the words in this passage that ground the question you just put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The words in this passage appear on the second page of the English version that say -- the last paragraph on the second page that says: "Since we are currently using this facility for the above purposes of transit accommodation of Muslim civilians, and we plan on continuing do so in the next period," and then continues to ask for resources to provide for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the question that you put was what?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Based on the date of the document and the assertion that they're currently using this facility for the purpose of transit of civilians, I felt I was able to ask -- to put the document to the witness who had said in 1993, 1994, 1995, he did not see civilians at Kula prison and ask whether or not he was -- he wished to change his testimony having seen the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not the question. The question included imprisoned civilians. This document shows that it was all done in cooperation with the commission. There was no mention of incarceration. That's one thing. And to help refugees to reach their apartments on the other side is another thing. It was done by the commission for the refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, my colleague has found the question, which is at page 78, line 12. It was an easy enough question. "Were there not civilians imprisoned at Kula along with these members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were detained there?" So there is no basis for putting that they were imprisoned because the document says that the facility was used for the purpose of transit accommodation. Later on apparently you did use the words "pass through," but perhaps now you can conclude by putting the question on the basis that the facility was used for transit, and ask the witness whether he can confirm or not confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll simply revert, actually, Your Honours, to my earlier question and the wording that I perhaps more properly used there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, seeing this document which affirms that Kula was, as of October 1994, used as a transit facility and that 10.000 Muslims of all ages had passed through there up until the period of 28 October 1994, do you still hold to your assertion that you didn't see any civilians there in 1993, 1994, or 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still hold to my assertion that in 1994 and 1995 I did not see a single civilian. It wasn't possible for me either. I could have seen some detainees. I know there were some detainees from the Serb army as well as from the Muslim army, and you could see them from my office because they would be taken outside for their regular exercise. I didn't see any civilians though. As for the other part of the question which specifies that 10.000 people went through the KPD Kula, I have to say that they had no means to accept so many people. I know that today, for example, the KPD Kula cannot house more than 120 detainees. It was not expanded since the wartime, and the figures you are mentioning are beyond their ability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now I must find out, Mr. Tapuskovic, are you re-examining, because we are not going beyond 12.45. Are you going to re-examine and, if so, for how long? Because you are now well past the time allotted to you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm aware, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I won't insist on keeping the witness here any longer just in order to re-examine him, although I would have certain questions. In any case, once we reach 12.45, I agree that we release the witness no matter how far we got. I'm even willing to set aside all of this remaining time to the -- for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I don't know whether she wants the rest of the time. One last question, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I use that to ask that this document be tendered as the next Prosecution exhibit, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document is P811.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an objection I wanted to make. This document speaks exclusively about the humanitarian aspect. This is why I object to it -- its admittance. I just wanted to mention, to underline, that this document speaks of a humanitarian activity in cooperation with humanitarian organisations in order to transport civilians to different parts of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So on that basis you're saying --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you saying, that on that basis, for that reason it's not relevant or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my position that it is irrelevant the way it was used by the Prosecutor in order to try and prove that civilians were being arrested. Civilians had to go through that facility in one way or another in order for them to be able to reach their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton. Ms. Edgerton, we admitted the document before Mr. Tapuskovic was able to make his objection, so I'd like to hear you now on the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The objection is on the basis of relevance, saying that I used it to try and prove that civilians were being arrested, Your Honour, as I understand it. And, Your Honour, the document when squarely, I would submit, put to the witness's testimony in chief and in cross-examination where he said, "He never in 1993, 1994, and 1995 saw civilians at Kula prison." I put this document to him without referring to the word "arrest" or "detention," it simply went to his assertion that he hadn't seen civilians, and it's a matter for his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Credibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Credibility, Mr. Tapuskovic, that's the basis on which the questions were put. So we admit it. I do understand then you have no re-examination? In which case --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has my learned friend finished?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You might have missed that, but she did indicate that she was finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we could perhaps clear something up. It had to do with the 31st of May, 1992 and the witness's answers. Re-examination by Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What was happening before the 31st of May, 1992, to the people who resided in Trnovo? What was happening before that? During the cross-examination, you said that on the 31st of May the VRS entered Trnovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Why did they have to enter turn Trnovo since before that time Serbs made up the majority of the population in Trnovo? What had happened before the 31st of May?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's a leading question, Your Honours, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, very leading. Very leading. Reformulate it, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What happened before the 31st of May, in the months preceding that date in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADE IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April and May 1992, in the area of Trnovo municipality, 90 per cent of the territory was controlled by the members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There are over 40 villages in that area, all of which had been surrounded by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As of the 3rd of June until the 7th of July, in those villages over 100 civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I chose not to rise initially, but when the evidence came to the time period past the 31st of May, 1992, I feel I should rise because that's not something that comes from my cross-examination. I would submit I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree. Let's conclude this, Mr. Tapuskovic. It doesn't arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, we'll adjourn and resume on Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I just have an indication with the next witness who would normally have appeared on the schedule, T-61?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who is the next witness, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The next witness is Witness T-61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I know everything I need to know now, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have your work cut out for you on the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 9th day of July, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.34 p.m.,
